summary:
### Key Topics Discussed
- Analysis of current code structure and its inability to handle logic efficiently.
- Prioritization of post-invoicing over subscription invoicing.
- Understanding of the order concept as a task factory and coordinator for data handling.
- Detailed analysis of the order concept product, specifically identifying information required for tasks.
- Definition of a task containing an article with its number and description.
- Importance of metadata, such as quantity, length, or size, being added to an article.
- Calculation of an article's value by multiplying its quantity with its unit price (e.g., per piece, per meter, or per hour).
- Consideration of production time for services and its impact on total time (e.g., 3 minutes per service for 10 items equals 30 minutes).
- Inclusion of cost as an additional metric for an article.
- Necessity of an execution code for tasks to determine assignment.
- Distinction between execution code and article type, where article type is for grouping (e.g., laundry, goods) and execution code is for task assignment.
- Requirement to attach geographical location (e.g., city, street, GPS coordinates) from the object to the task.
- Importance of geographical resolution for object location, from high-resolution GPS coordinates to less precise city information.
- Introduction of time factors within the order concept, including one or more time windows.
- Definition of a main time window with desired delivery times (start and end times for job completion).
- Ability to add additional stops or more favorable times based on metadata within the order concept.
- Discussion of soft time windows (e.g., advantageous days like Thursdays and Fridays) and hard time stops (e.g., prohibited days like Mondays).
- The role of a time engine in optimizing task scheduling based on time specifications.
- Handling of time window expiration in gross planning, where tasks are moved to the next available time or generate a warning if all windows are passed, making the article "red" or un-deliverable.
- "Clustering" of tasks in gross planning based on location, time, and type to facilitate assignment, focusing on "what, where, and when" tasks should be done.
- Integration of order concept with invoicing: tasks are completed and then combined into one or more invoices.
- Monthly invoicing results in a parallel track of invoices.
- Consideration of combined invoicing for fixed monthly billing and additional services, where a zero-value invoice confirms task completion against prepayments, but additional orders result in charges.
- Dynamic updating is crucial for long-term schedules, including price changes (updated price lists) and changes in the number or type of items/tasks at an object.
- Invoicing within the order concept: invoices are created for the customer at the top of the cluster with the same invoice references.
- All tasks created under an order should inherit the invoice reference (e.g., "Vårtvätten 2026").
- Invoicing frequency can be set (e.g., weekly invoicing) or automatically triggered per completed task. There is also an option for invoices to be gathered per object.
- The order concept can consist of tasks with different execution types, and the customer might not want too many invoices.
- The system will hold invoicing until all tasks related to different execution types (e.g., cleaning different types of bins) within an order are completed. This solution is considered suitable for larger customers.
- Invoice references can be replaced by metadata fields like area code, property designation, or cost center, depending on customer preference.
- Tasks will be marked with attached information such as customer name and property number (e.g., "Anna Karlsson - fastighetsnummer 123") instead of a general project number.
- Invoicing rules: partial invoicing is allowed if permitted, otherwise all tasks must be completed before invoicing. For weekly or monthly collective invoices, the system waits for the invoicing period to end.
- Date determination for invoicing: RepliQ needs to determine the exact date, with one option being the order concept creation date plus one month.
- Explanation of "invoice top level" as the information in the invoice header.
- Discussion of how invoicing for a customer like Anna Karlsson, who manages multiple properties, could result in multiple invoices, potentially one per property, with the invoice information needing to be clearly defined at the "FakturaToppen" (invoice top level).
- Introduction of invoice references at the line item level, following the same logic as the metadata available to the executor.
- Attachment of specific metadata to tasks for each article line, such as "fasadnummer" (facade number) and "färg på soptunnan" (color of the waste bin), linked to when the task was performed.
- Logic requirement: If multiple tasks share the same metadata reference from an object, the metadata should not be repeated for each task.

### Decisions Made
- Postpone work on subscription invoicing to focus on post-invoicing.

### Action Items
- RepliQ needs to analyze the current code structure to understand why it cannot handle the required logic.
- Jointly analyze the order concept product to create a list of information that tasks should contain.
- Summarize the requirements for tasks to ensure Trymo understands them.
- A "place engine" must be created to optimize geographical data based on available information and metadata.
- RepliQ to define the business rule for invoicing dates, e.g., the date an order concept was created or executed plus one month, or the last day of the current month for monthly invoicing.

### Important Points & Insights
- The current code structure is inadequate for efficient logic handling.
- The order concept, whether for subscriptions or single tasks, acts as a task factory and coordinator, ensuring all necessary data is attached to tasks.
- Tasks will be used in many different ways, requiring careful consideration of the information they contain.
- A key component of a task is an article, well-defined by its article number and description.
- Articles will need associated metadata like quantity, length, or size.
- The value of an article is determined by its quantity multiplied by its unit price or time.
- Production time and cost are crucial factors to consider for services.
- The execution code is crucial for task distribution.
- Article type serves an administrative grouping function and is different from the execution code.
- Geographical location is a critical piece of information to attach from the object, with varying levels of precision from GPS coordinates to city names.
- The order concept can include time windows, with a primary window for desired delivery and options to add more stops or optimize times based on metadata.
- Time windows can be soft (preferred times) or hard (prohibited times).
- A time engine will use these time specifications to find the most advantageous time for task execution.
- Expired time windows will cause articles to be marked as undeliverable.
- Gross planning will utilize a geography-optimization engine to cluster tasks that are geographically close, time-feasible, and of the same type for efficient assignment.
- An order, as a collective request, becomes an order concept which then splits into numerous tasks, including dependent tasks.
- Completed tasks are eventually consolidated into invoices, with monthly invoicing creating a separate invoicing stream.
- For monthly billing, customers will receive a monthly invoice based on the order concept, followed by zero-value confirmation invoices for each task completed, balancing against the prepaid amount. Any additional services not covered by the fixed monthly fee will be itemized and charged on these confirmation invoices. If a customer wishes to incorporate an extra job into the fixed billing, it can be added to the regular invoicing to avoid separate charges.
- Dynamic updates are essential for long-term schedules, especially concerning administrative price changes and modifications in the number or type of recurring tasks at a specific location.
- The schema (scheduling) will be addressed in the next step.
- All tasks generated under an order, stemming from a customer (e.g., Anna Karlsson), must include a specific invoice reference (e.g., project number "Vårtvätten 2026").
- Invoicing can be set to weekly or triggered immediately upon task completion. There is also an option to consolidate invoices "per object" to avoid excessive individual invoices.
- Invoice references on tasks can be replaced by specific metadata fields (e.g., area code, property designation, cost center).
- Tasks will be marked with detailed property information (e.g., "fastighetsnummer 123") rather than a single project reference.
- Invoicing typically occurs when the job is done or, alternatively, through monthly invoicing. An exception is incorrect eco-invoicing.
- The invoice top level refers to the information in the invoice header, including customer, reference (e.g., from an invoice recipient), invoice concept, and customer's reference (e.g., Anna Karlsson, Vårtvätten 2026, or property reference via metadata).
- It is possible to replace customer name (Anna Karlsson) with a metadata reference.
- The list of completed tasks will become more complex with these metadata changes.
- Invoice top-level information must be explicitly defined and sorted, especially when a customer (e.g., Anna Karlsson) is responsible for multiple properties, potentially leading to separate invoices per property.
- Invoice references at the line-item level (radnivå) will use the same metadata logic available to the executor.
- For each article line, three pieces of information will be associated: when the task was performed, the facade number, and the color of the waste bin.
- A logic is needed to prevent redundant metadata entries if multiple tasks on an object share the same metadata reference.

### Open Questions/Pending Items
- Clarify how the cost metric is specifically calculated and applied within the system.
